solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Charlie's time here in ancient Rome average, on reflection

parts.note: hic is the Latin word for here, the language of ancient Rome

indicators.note: a reflection shows a thing back to front, so the word for average is read backwards

parts.note: OK means fair to middling, just average

explanation.surface: Someone muses about Charlie's ordinary stay in ancient Rome, looking back on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' turns OK into KO. A charlie is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for a stupid person; a charlie is a dimwit or idiot.

clue.text: Noble, with great success, recited poetic lines

indicators.note: something recited is spoken, so the words are judged by how they sound

parts.note: noble means high-born, HIGH, and a great success is a COUP, said as 'coo'

explanation.surface: An aristocrat, after a triumph, reads verse aloud to an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: HIGH plus COUP, spoken, gives the Japanese verse form.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese verse form of three short lines, seventeen syllables in all.

clue.text: That French pooch barking extremely noisily, makes din

parts.note: ça is French for that

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the word pooch is jumbled
extremely points to the extreme letters, first and last, of noisily

explanation.surface: A French dog yapping loudly is making a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barking' rearranges POOCH into COPHO; 'extremely' takes N and Y from noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a harsh, discordant mixture of loud sounds.

clue.text: Recently, Zoe defaced nursing uniform

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the trimmed name wraps around the other piece
defaced means losing the face, here the front letter of the name Zoe

parts.note: flat as in a flat rate: uniform, the same throughout

explanation.surface: Zoe has lately vandalised a nurse's uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defaced' removes the name's first letter, and 'nursing' makes what is left hold the other piece. 'uniform' looks like clothing but means even.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs for something happening lately, in the recent past.

clue.text: He and Nora munched, grabbing salt and pepper

indicators.note: grabbing means holding onto, so the scrambled letters close around the sailor
food that is munched is chewed up, so the letters of He and Nora are mixed

parts.note: an old salt is a sailor, and AB (able seaman) is a sailor in crosswords

explanation.surface: Two diners eat their meal and reach for the salt and pepper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'munched' scrambles the two names into HANERO, and 'grabbing' closes it round the sailor. 'salt and pepper' looks like the cruet pair, but salt is the sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A habanero is a very hot chilli, a kind of capsicum pepper.

clue.text: Religious type, one with seat in Ireland, unified states once

parts.note: holy means devout or sacred
roman is a typeface, the upright style of print

indicators.note: in places the member of parliament inside the Irish name

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland
an MP holds a seat in parliament

explanation.surface: A devout person with a parliamentary seat in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unified states once' points to the past; 'type' is a printing term, not a kind of person.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose union of central European territories that lasted from medieval times until 1806.

clue.text: Standing erect, head of trawler discarded sprat

indicators.note: discarded means thrown away, so the trawler's front letter is dropped

parts.note: bristling describes hairs standing up on end

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A fish thrown back by the trawler skipper stands up stiffly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discarded' drops T from BRISTLING.
explanation.definitionFit: A brisling is a small sprat, often canned as a sardine.

clue.text: Runner's spirit rising, about to be uplifted

indicators.note: in a down entry something rising reads from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: gin is a spirit

indicators.note: uplifted in a down entry means turned upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: An athlete's morale lifts, about to be raised up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns GIN into NIG and 'to be uplifted' turns RE into ER. A runner in crosswords is often a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river runs, so crossword setters call it a runner; this is the great West African river.

clue.text: Free gift's first choice, taken up as top bit of property

parts.note: to rid is to free or clear

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
taken up in a down entry means lifted, reading upwards and so backwards

parts.note: the elite is the choice, the pick of the bunch

explanation.surface: A free gift is picked and taken away from a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' turns ELITE into ETILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A roofing piece that caps the apex of a house roof, its highest part.

clue.text: Gather a flower when rambling, and preserve

indicators.note: rambling speech runs words together carelessly, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: to gather a flower is to pick a lily, run together in speech

explanation.surface: A walker picks a flower while out on a ramble, then presses it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when rambling' signals that PICK A LILY, gabbled, sounds like the pickle. 'rambling' and 'preserve' suggest a country walk and pressed flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A preserve here is a pickle or relish; this is a mustard pickle of chopped vegetables.

clue.text: Work with surgeon in part of theatre

parts.note: to go is to work or function, as in the machine won't go
DS is the abbreviation for Doctor of Surgery

explanation.surface: Someone works alongside a surgeon in an operating theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' suggests the operating theatre but means a playhouse. The gods are its highest gallery seats.
explanation.definitionFit: The gods is the colloquial name for the top gallery, the cheapest seats high in a playhouse.

clue.text: Comedian not initially fit, needing rest for a change

indicators.note: not initially means without its opening letter

parts.note: to equip is to fit out

indicators.note: for a change means altered, so the letters of rest are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tired comic who is not fit at first needs a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not initially' drops E from EQUIP, and 'for a change' turns REST into STER.
explanation.definitionFit: A quipster is a maker of witty remarks, a joker or wag.

clue.text: Left with hours wasted in comparatively grim place to refuel

indicators.note: wasted means lost, so the letter for hours is dropped

parts.note: harder is the comparative of hard, meaning grim or harsh

explanation.surface: Someone left waiting hours in a grimmer place to refuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasted' removes H from HARDER. 'refuel' suggests a petrol station; here a person refuels with food.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a pantry where food is kept, so a person replenishes themselves there.

clue.text: Loves to smother trout's skin in aromatic oil

indicators.note: to smother is to cover over, so the two loves wrap around the fish's skin

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written O, so loves gives two Os

indicators.note: a word's skin is its outer letters, first and last

explanation.surface: Fish is wrapped in fragrant oil for cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: TT, the outer letters of TROUT, sit between two Os.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, or attar, is a fragrant essential oil from rose petals.

clue.text: Single's original released by Rod Stewart sadly failed to progress

indicators.note: sadly means badly or wretchedly, so the remaining letters are rearranged
released means let go, so the single's first letter is let out of the singer's name
the original of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A record from rock singer Rod Stewart flopped in the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'released by' drops S from RODSTEWART and 'sadly' rearranges the rest. 'Single' looks like a record, but only gives its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread water is an idiom for staying in place without advancing.

clue.text: American child one leaves somewhere in Bavaria with family

indicators.note: leaves means departs, so the one goes out of the city

parts.note: Munich is the capital of Bavaria
I is the Roman numeral one
kin are relatives, family

explanation.surface: An American kid departs a Bavarian town with relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' removes I from MUNICH.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US munchkin is informal for a small child, after the little people of Oz.

clue.text: That man on pottery course is an author

parts.note: he is that man
Ming is the fine Chinese porcelain of the Ming dynasty
a way is a course or route

explanation.surface: A man doing a ceramics course turns out to be a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' simply joins HE to the next pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway is the American novelist who wrote The Old Man and the Sea.

clue.text: Wise person in US city beginning to talk in bygone language

indicators.note: in means placed within, so the bird goes inside the city's letters

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
an owl is proverbially wise, so a wise person is an owl

indicators.note: beginning to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A sage in an American city starts speaking in an old tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'in' is taken as it is, giving letters, while the first places the bird inside the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Low Latin is the popular, post-classical Latin of the late Roman and medieval period, no longer spoken.

clue.text: Old place to learn, with Australian, about an aquatic invertebrate

parts.note: a poly was a British polytechnic, a college before most became universities in 1992

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the Australian letters are reversed

parts.note: Oz is slang for Australia and Australian

explanation.surface: A former college and an Australian are studying a water creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns OZ into ZO. A poly was a British polytechnic.
explanation.definitionFit: A polyzoan is a bryozoan, a tiny colonial water animal with no backbone.

clue.text: Appearance of pigeons at regular intervals, miles ahead

indicators.note: ahead puts the miles letter in front of the others
at regular intervals means every other letter of pigeons

explanation.surface: Pigeons are seen at regular intervals, miles out in front.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of pigeons give IEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Mien is a person's look or bearing, their outward aspect.

clue.text: Scavenger, one among crew most of all

parts.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, one of a ship's crew

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter

explanation.surface: A scavenging animal is the biggest of all among a pack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the last L of ALL to leave AL.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackal is a wild dog that lives largely by eating carrion.

clue.text: Type of chair from Westminster area, with exotic brass turning

parts.note: SW1 is the London postcode for Westminster, the 1 read as I

indicators.note: turning means reversing direction, so the currency is read backwards

parts.note: brass is slang for money; the lev is Bulgarian currency, foreign money

explanation.surface: A chair from Westminster, fitted with fancy brass, spins round.
explanation.walkthrough: SW1 is the postcode around Parliament, with the 1 taken as I. 'turning' reverses the currency, giving VEL; 'brass' is slang for money, not the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A swivel chair turns on a pivot, so the word names that kind of seat.

clue.text: Bilious woman needing some Kleenex I've passed over

indicators.note: passed over in a down entry means turned upward, reading backwards
some means a part, so the letters lie within the words

explanation.surface: A queasy woman needs a few of the tissues I've handed across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks NEXIV from Kleenex I've and 'passed over' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A vixen is a bad-tempered, spiteful woman, as bilious can mean peevish.

clue.text: Sordid property chap's seen around English headland

indicators.note: seen around means placed around, so the chap's letters enclose the English letter

parts.note: a chap is a man
a ness is a headland or promontory

explanation.surface: A seedy house belonging to a man near an English cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'property' suggests real estate but here means a quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Meanness is the quality of being base or shabby, a sordid trait.

clue.text: Financiers are here on business, following special painting

indicators.note: following puts the City pieces after the special letter

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London, the financial district
CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: Bankers are here on a special business trip.
explanation.walkthrough: EC is the City of London postcode, home of British finance.
explanation.definitionFit: Secco is wall painting done on dry plaster, as opposed to fresco on wet.

clue.text: By place to keep animals, cross underground river

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: Someone crosses an underground river beside a farm pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Styx is the river of the underworld.

clue.text: Expect judge perhaps to hesitate

parts.note: expect and judge can each mean think, so the clue states that verb two times over, and the phrase means pause to reconsider

explanation.surface: A judge, perhaps, should expect to hesitate.
explanation.walkthrough: Expect and judge each mean THINK, so the clue's two words are THINK given twice.
explanation.definitionFit: To think twice is an idiom for pausing to reconsider before acting.

clue.text: Gold steps outside new store for big guns?

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the steps wrap around the letter for new

parts.note: a dance is a set of steps

explanation.surface: Golden steps lead outside a fresh depot holding heavy guns.
explanation.walkthrough: N inside DANCE gives DANNCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance means military stores and artillery, the supply of heavy weapons.

clue.text: Overthrow secular base

parts.note: lay means not of the clergy, secular
low means base or vulgar

explanation.surface: Toppling a worldly foundation.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring down or defeat is an idiom using these two words.
